newsitem.title: ALBANIA: South Albania town fights lawlessness.
newsitem.headline: South Albania town fights lawlessness.

text.p: A gang drove into the Albanian town of Delvine at midnight on Friday and robbed the local bank, using a tow-truck and winch to rip the vault from its foundations and drag it away down the street.
Delvine's Mayor, Pellumb Ibrahimi, couldn't help noticing. His flat sits in the bank building, directly above the void where the vault once stood.
"The noise woke me. The robbers drove into town and circled the square firing Kalashnikovs in the air to warn people to stay away while they did their work," the Mayor recalled.
"These were not local men. They were a gang from Sarande. Our town is calm except for outside influences."

The recent collapse of a number of pyramid schemes in Albania bankrupted many families, plunged the country into political crisis and provoked widespread civil unrest -- especially in the south where pyramid losses were greatest.
Southern Albania has since become synonymous with a wacky brand of banditry. public and private property are looted with abandon.
With no police or army to restrain them, gunmen are roaming the south looking for targets in sleepy towns like Delvine, population 9,000.
The nearby port of Sarande, long a smugglers' paradise given its proximity to the Greek island of Corfu and to Italy, is one of the main centres for gang activity.

Thugs from Sarande cruise the region in their late model Mercedes and BMW's, wearing leather jackets and carrying Kalashnikovs, hand grenades and rocket-propelled grenade launchers stolen from Albanian army barracks.
Delvine, nestled in the hills 20 miles (30 Km) inland from Sarande, is trying to turn its back on this madness.

"Our local council met and issued orders that teenagers are forbidden to possess guns and asking that all heavy weapons including tanks and artillery pieces, be surrendered to public control or returned to barracks," Mayor Ibrahimi said.
"Generally, there has been compliance. We have had no deaths here, accidental or intentional. However, the gangs from places like Sarande are out of control. The bank robbery was proof of that."
Once the Ottoman administrative centre for all of southern Albania, Delvine has been overshadowed in modern times by Sarande's rapid growth and by Gjirokaster, the region's new administrative hub.

But five years ago Greek investors opened a textile factory in Delvine employing 250 local residents and giving the town an investment in the future which few communities its size in Albania -- Europe's poorest country -- can boast.
Perhaps for that reason townspeople have drawn the line at the mindless violence sweeping much of the south. When gangs came to loot Delvine's textile factory residents and workers drove them away.
The factory remains in operation and is shipping its product, under armed guard, by truck to the Greek border.
"The factory workers are getting paid and that is helping us to survive these days," said 45-year old Bilal Kohila, a Delvine resident.

"We have electricity and water and our hospital and bakery are functioning. But teachers and town public employees and pensioners are not getting paid. And there is this violence, not in our town, but around it, which worries us."

The Mayor said that the representatives from 10 political parties participating in Delvine's local council are united in their support for the new coalition government formed two weeks ago in Tirana under Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

"The members of the council are from different parties but we are agreed in one aim, and that is to preserve peace and order in our town," the Mayor said. "That single goal is more important than all of our political differences."
"There are no gangs here. Some in Delvine blame President (Sali) Berisha for the pyramid schemes but even they are not rebels against the (Fino) government of National Salvation.
"We think of ourselves as Albanians living in difficult times."
